newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar up more than half yen in Tokyo after summit.
newsitem.headline: Dollar up more than half yen in Tokyo after summit.

text.p: The dollar gained more than half a yen by midday Tokyo on Monday compared to its Friday New York close level as the economic statement at the G7 summit failed to reinforce worries about Japan's rising trade surplus.
"Operators felt comfortable about buying dollars during the morning since the tone of the G7 statement about Japan's surplus was weak," said a senior Tokyo dealer.
The dollar ended at around 114.85 yen in Friday New York.

Saturday's economic statement by the G7 -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the U.S. -- said only that Japan has the objective of achieving strong domestic demand-led growth and avoiding a significant rise in its external surplus.
A senior Tokyo official attending the summit in Denver, Colorado, told Reuters that the G7 agreed on nothing more or less on currencies than their finance ministers did in April.
"Supply-and-demand conditions in the spot currency market look to have turned in favour of dollar buying," said another Japanese bank dealer.
Japanese trust banks bought dollars and marks against the yen, probably on behalf of pension funds who planned to invest fresh money in foreign stocks and bonds.
Overseas funds, including U.S. funds, also moved to buy dollars, although some cashed in profits after its rise.
Japanese exporters, who had been keen to sell dollars until last week, slowed down their dollar-selling activity as worries about U.S.-Japan trade friction faded.
"Although the problem of Japan's trade surplus has not been wiped out completely, fears of political pressure to guide the yen higher could subside for a while," said one dealer.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin denied on Saturday that the United States was toning down its criticism of Japan over Tokyo's rising trade surplus, but admitted that the issue was not the main focus of meeting there.
"I don't think that issue was downplayed or up-played," Rubin told reporters.
A U.S. bank dealer said since the dollar was able to rise above a technical resistance point of 115.50 yen, it is expected to move into the 115.50-117.00 yen range.
Many dealers said if the dollar rises above 115.80 yen, an upward trend for the dollar could be confirmed.
Dealers said expectations that the Bank of Japan's "tankan" corporate survey, due out on Wednesday, could show weak business sentiment, have supported the dollar.
One dealer said a weak tankan result has not been fully factored into the market and thus the dollar may get a further boost if the survey comes in as weak as anticipated.
